summary: Psalm 99 announces that Yahweh reigns, so the peoples and the earth are summoned to respond with awe. It praises God as holy, just, and exalted, then remembers Moses, Aaron, and Samuel as people who called on Yahweh and were answered. The psalm ends by calling worshipers to exalt Yahweh at his holy hill because he is holy.
whyItMatters: Within Book IV of Psalms, this chapter belongs to the repeated emphasis that Yahweh reigns. It links God's kingship with justice, worship, answered prayer, forgiveness, and accountability.

context.author: Psalms is an anthology by many writers and collections; this psalm has no author named in the chapter text.
context.audience: Israel's worshiping and instructed community, later received by Jewish and Christian communities for public prayer and private reading.
context.date: Individual psalms may preserve material from the monarchy through the postexilic period, but assigning one date to the whole Psalter or this chapter from this chapter alone would be misleading.
context.setting: Book IV of Psalms, where the collection emphasizes Yahweh's kingship, creation, memory, and enduring mercy after the crisis of earlier royal hopes.
context.literaryForm: Compressed Hebrew poetry and worship speech, using repeated calls to praise and worship, remembered figures from Israel's past, and the refrain-like declaration that God is holy.

outline.heading: The reigning king
outline.note: Yahweh reigns, sits enthroned among the cherubim, and is great in Zion above all peoples.

outline.heading: Praise the holy name
outline.note: The peoples are called to praise God's great and awesome name because he is holy.

outline.heading: Justice in Jacob
outline.note: The King's strength is described as loving justice, establishing equity, and executing justice and righteousness.

outline.heading: Worship at his footstool
outline.note: The worshiping community is told to exalt Yahweh and worship at his footstool because he is holy.

outline.heading: Answered callers
outline.note: Moses, Aaron, and Samuel are remembered as people who called on Yahweh; the psalm says he answered, spoke, gave statutes, forgave, and also held doings accountable.

outline.heading: Worship at his holy hill
outline.note: The final call repeats the summons to exalt and worship, now at God's holy hill, because Yahweh is holy.

keyVerses.text: Yahweh reigns! Let the peoples tremble. He sits enthroned among the cherubim. Let the earth be moved.
keyVerses.why: This opening line gives the chapter its center: Yahweh's kingship is not private or local only, but affects peoples and earth.

keyVerses.text: The King’s strength also loves justice. You establish equity. You execute justice and righteousness in Jacob.
keyVerses.why: The verse defines divine kingship in moral terms: strength is joined to justice, equity, and righteousness.

keyVerses.text: Moses and Aaron were among his priests, Samuel was among those who call on his name. They called on Yahweh, and he answered them.
keyVerses.why: The psalm turns from general praise to remembered figures who called on Yahweh and were answered.

keyVerses.text: You answered them, Yahweh our God. You are a God who forgave them, although you took vengeance for their doings.
keyVerses.why: This verse holds together two claims the chapter does not separate: God answered and forgave, and God also dealt seriously with wrongdoing.

themes: Yahweh's reign over peoples and earth
Kingship joined to justice and equity
Worship at God's footstool and holy hill

questions.question: What is the main claim of Psalm 99?
questions.answer: The chapter's main claim is that Yahweh reigns. The opening verse announces his rule, and the rest of the psalm explains that rule through holiness, justice, worship, answered prayer, forgiveness, and accountability.

questions.question: Why does the psalm say the peoples should tremble and the earth be moved?
questions.answer: The language presents Yahweh's reign as weighty and world-affecting. The response is awe before the one enthroned among the cherubim and exalted above all peoples, not a casual admiration of a local ruler.

questions.question: What are the cherubim?
questions.answer: The chapter says Yahweh sits enthroned among the cherubim, but it does not explain them. Within this psalm, the phrase functions as throne-room language: Yahweh is pictured as reigning from a holy, exalted place.

questions.question: What does Zion mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: Psalm 99 says, "Yahweh is great in Zion." The chapter later speaks of worship at God's holy hill, so Zion functions here as the worship-centered place associated with Yahweh's greatness and holiness.

questions.question: How does the chapter connect kingship and justice?
questions.answer: Verse 4 does not describe the King only as powerful. It says his strength loves justice, establishes equity, and executes justice and righteousness in Jacob, so rule and right judgment belong together in the psalm's portrait of God.

questions.question: Why are Moses, Aaron, and Samuel named?
questions.answer: They are named as figures associated with priestly service or calling on Yahweh's name. The psalm uses them as examples of people who called on Yahweh and were answered, then adds that they kept his testimonies and the statute he gave them.

questions.question: How can God forgive and also take vengeance for doings?
questions.answer: Verse 8 places both statements side by side: Yahweh answered and forgave them, although he took vengeance for their doings. Readers differ on whether "them" points only to the named leaders, to the people connected with them, or to the community remembered through them, but the verse itself holds forgiveness and accountability together.

questions.question: What does the repeated line “He is Holy” do in the psalm?
questions.answer: The declaration appears after calls to praise or worship and returns at the end as the reason for worship at God's holy hill. Its repetition gives the chapter a refrain-like structure and keeps holiness at the center of God's reign, justice, and mercy.

questions.question: Does Psalm 99 say readers should copy ancient worship practices directly?
questions.answer: The psalm calls its worshiping audience to exalt Yahweh and worship at his footstool and holy hill. It describes ancient worship language within Israel's prayer book; later Jewish and Christian communities have received it in different worship settings, but the chapter itself does not lay out a modern policy or ritual procedure.

glossary.def: Heavenly throne-associated beings named in verse 1; in this chapter they mark Yahweh's enthroned rule.
The place named in verse 2 where Yahweh is said to be great; verse 9's holy hill language keeps the focus on worship and God's holiness.
The place where worshipers are told to worship in verse 5; the word supports the psalm's picture of Yahweh as enthroned king.
The form in which verse 7 says Yahweh spoke to the remembered leaders; the chapter uses it as part of Israel's memory of divine speech.
What verse 7 says the remembered leaders kept, paired with the statute Yahweh gave them.
